studio.title: Arduino Studio: ATmega328P Firmware, ADC, PWM and UART
studio.intro: Arduino Studio runs your sketch against a virtual Uno board with LEDs, a push button, a potentiometer, sensors, an LCD and a serial console. Behind every call such as analogRead or analogWrite sits a peripheral of the ATmega328P with its own arithmetic.
studio.purpose: The studio has a single workspace rather than separate modes: a code editor, the board canvas with mountable sensors, a speed selector ($0.5\times$, $1\times$, $2\times$ or instant) and a serial console. This document explains the hardware that your code controls, so you can predict pin levels, ADC counts, PWM frequencies and baud rates before you run the sketch.

model.heading: ATmega328P architecture
model.body: The Uno uses an 8-bit AVR core with a Harvard architecture, clocked by a crystal at $f_{clk} = 16\text{ MHz}$, so one machine cycle lasts $t_{clk} = 62.5\text{ ns}$. It offers $32\text{ KB}$ of flash for the program, $2\text{ KB}$ of SRAM and $1\text{ KB}$ of EEPROM. Three timers ($\texttt{Timer0}$, $\texttt{Timer1}$, $\texttt{Timer2}$), a 10-bit ADC with six channels, a USART and two external interrupt pins ($\texttt{INT0}$ on pin $2$ and $\texttt{INT1}$ on pin $3$) are the peripherals the studio models.

model.heading: 10-bit successive-approximation ADC
model.body: The converter compares the input with a binary-weighted reference, one bit per clock, over ten steps. With a reference $V_{ref} = 5\text{ V}$ one step is $V_{step} = V_{ref}/1024 \approx 4.88\text{ mV}$, and the datasheet code is $\lfloor 1024\,V_{in}/V_{ref} \rfloor$ saturated at $1023$. A convention matters here: the studio, like many teaching tools, maps full scale to code $1023$ using $\lfloor V_{in} \cdot 1023/V_{ref} \rfloor$, so $V_{in} = 5\text{ V}$ gives exactly $1023$. The two forms differ by at most one count. Both truncate, never round, so the quantization error is between $0$ and $-1$ LSB.

model.heading: Timer PWM modes and prescaler
model.body: analogWrite loads the compare register $\texttt{OCRnA}$ or $\texttt{OCRnB}$ with a value from $0$ to $255$. In Fast PWM the counter climbs to $255$ and resets, so $f = f_{clk}/(N \cdot 256)$ and the duty cycle is $(\texttt{OCRnx}+1)/256$. In Phase-Correct PWM the counter climbs and then falls, which gives $f = f_{clk}/(N \cdot 510)$ and a duty cycle of $\texttt{OCRnx}/255$, with symmetric pulses and less switching noise. The prescaler divides the clock by $N \in \{1, 8, 64, 256, 1024\}$. On an Uno the Arduino core selects $N = 64$ for the timers it uses for analogWrite: pins $5$ and $6$ run Fast PWM at about $977\text{ Hz}$, and pins $9$ and $10$ run Phase-Correct at about $490\text{ Hz}$, as do pins $3$ and $11$.

model.heading: External interrupts and UART
model.body: attachInterrupt links an ISR to a pin edge on $\texttt{INT0}$ or $\texttt{INT1}$. The hardware needs at least four cycles, about $0.25\text{ }\mu\text{s}$, before the first ISR instruction, and variables shared with loop must be declared $\texttt{volatile}$. The USART divides the clock with $\text{UBRR} = f_{osc}/(16 \cdot \text{Baud}) - 1$, rounded to an integer, so the real rate differs from the request by the error $e$ shown above. Errors beyond roughly $2\text{ percent}$ make frames unreliable. The studio models the serial console and reports the baud passed to Serial.begin; its interrupt handling is a concept to practise on real hardware.

mapping.body: Sweeping the knob changes $V_{in}$ from $0$ to $V_{ref}$, and analogRead returns $\lfloor V_{in} \cdot 1023/V_{ref} \rfloor$.
Ranges from $0$ to $100\,^\circ\text{C}$ at $10\text{ mV}/{}^\circ\text{C}$, so each ADC count is about $0.49\,^\circ\text{C}$.
A logarithmic slider from $0.1$ to $10000\text{ lux}$ sets $R_{LDR}$, forming a divider with a $10\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor to ground.
Distance from $2$ to $400\text{ cm}$ becomes an echo pulse of $58.2\text{ }\mu\text{s}$ per centimetre, which pulseIn measures.
The PIR output is HIGH for a hold time of $1$ to $5\text{ s}$; the IR output is active LOW at or inside a threshold from $1$ to $30\text{ cm}$.
analogWrite accepts $0$ to $255$; the board shows the duty $\texttt{OCRnx}/255$ as LED brightness and in the pin tooltip.
Shows the baud given to Serial.begin, such as $9600$ or $115200$, and lets you send text back to the sketch.
Scales sketch execution by $0.5\times$, $1\times$ or $2\times$ so you can follow delay-based timing, or runs instantly.

example.title: LM35 reading, PWM rate and baud choice
example.problem: An LM35 at $T = 25\,^\circ\text{C}$ feeds $\texttt{A0}$ with $V_{ref} = 5\text{ V}$. Find the ADC count, the temperature the sketch recovers, the PWM frequencies on pins $6$ and $9$, and the UART setting for $9600$ baud at $16\text{ MHz}$.

example.result: The sketch sees $\text{ADC} = 51$, which it converts to $24.9\,^\circ\text{C}$ (a $0.1\,^\circ\text{C}$ truncation loss). Pin $6$ switches at $976.6\text{ Hz}$ and pin $9$ at $490.2\text{ Hz}$. Setting $\text{UBRR} = 103$ gives an error of only $+0.16\%$, so $9600$ baud is reliable. By contrast $115200$ baud rounds to $\text{UBRR} = 8$ with $e = -3.55\%$, which is too large.

applications.body: Ultrasonic and IR sensors on an AVR give obstacle distance, and PWM drives motor speed through an H-bridge.
LM35 and LDR readings control fans and lamps, with thresholds set on the ADC code.
Serial links at a verified baud rate stream sensor data to a supervisory computer.
Timer PWM at a chosen $N$ generates the switching signal of a buck converter controller.
A PIR sensor wired to an external interrupt wakes the microcontroller only when motion occurs, saving energy.
